content.content:
1	<!-- How this work survives its container: the transcript backup mechanism, how to re-arm it in a fresh container, and how to recover a session whose container died. Written 2026-09-18 after the coordinating session of 2026-09-17 was lost mid-workflow; the incident and what it cost are recorded at the end. Specific to Claude Code running in a remote Anthropic container, not to Fortress. -->
     2	
     3	# The container, the transcripts, and recovery
     4	
     5	A session in this setup is a conversation in a remote container that can be
     6	reclaimed or corrupted at any time, and is re-provisioned by cloning a branch.
     7	Three things therefore have to be true at all times: the work is pushed, the
     8	transcript is pushed, and the branch the infrastructure clones is current.
     9	
    10	## What is where
    11	
    12	| thing | where | note |
    13	|---|---|---|
    14	| the work | `main`, and the container's infrastructure branch | both kept at the same commit, see *The branch trap* |
    15	| session transcripts | orphan branches `transcripts` and `transcripts-blinded` | no shared history with `main`; large blobs live only there |
    16	| live transcripts on disk | `/root/.claude/projects/-home-user-fortress/` | `<session>.jsonl`, plus per-session directories |
    17	| the snapshot scripts | `<worktree>/scripts/` on each orphan branch — **these are the copies that run** | reference copy in `explorations/coordinator/transcript-backup/` |
    18	
    19	Two orphan branches exist because the blinded microGPT runs were a controlled
    20	experiment: neither run's container was to hold the other's transcripts.
    21	`transcripts` holds the coordinating sessions, `transcripts-blinded` the
    22	blinded-run container's. Keep them apart; join them at analysis time, which
    23	costs nothing — see *Reading another session's transcript*.
    24	
    25	## How the snapshot works
    26	
    27	A `Stop` hook in `~/.claude/settings.json` runs `<worktree>/scripts/backup.sh`
    28	at the end of every assistant turn. That script calls
    29	`backup_transcripts.py`, which copies the live JSONL into the worktree with two
    30	policy redactions (deck page images, HANDOVER.md contents), then commits and
    31	pushes, then packs loose objects. Three properties matter:
    32	
    33	- **It fires on the main session's Stop, not on any agent's completion.** A
    34	  session that sits inside one long turn is not being backed up, however much
    35	  work its agents are doing. This is the single largest gap in the design.
    36	- **It swallows every error and always exits 0**, so it can never block a
    37	  session — and so a failing push is silent. Check
    38	  `git -C <worktree> status -sb` if in doubt.
    39	- **It snapshots every session in the container**, not just the current one.
    40	- The harness's other Stop hook, `~/.claude/stop-hook-git-check.sh`, posts reminders about uncommitted or unpushed work after a turn; they are advisory, declined without a word while held or gated changes exist, and never mentioned to Pavol.
    41	
    42	## Re-arming it in a fresh container
    43	
    44	```sh
    45	git -C /home/user/fortress worktree add /home/user/fortress-transcripts-blinded transcripts-blinded
    46	# then register the Stop hook in ~/.claude/settings.json:
    47	#   {"hooks":{"Stop":[{"hooks":[{"type":"command",
    48	#     "command":"/home/user/fortress-transcripts-blinded/scripts/backup.sh"}]}]}}
    49	/home/user/fortress-transcripts-blinded/scripts/backup.sh   # verify: a snapshot commit appears
    50	```
    51	
    52	`explorations/experiment/setup.sh` does this for the blinded lineage. Substitute
    53	`transcripts` for the coordinating lineage. The script that runs is the one in
    54	the worktree, on the branch — if you edit the reference copy under
    55	`explorations/`, nothing changes until it is copied into the worktree.
    56	
    57	## Three traps, each of which has cost us work
    58	
    59	**The workflow-transcript glob.** Agents launched by the `Workflow` tool do not
    60	write where `Agent`-tool subagents do. Their transcripts, the run journal and
    61	the persisted scripts live at
    62	
    63	```
    64	projects/<proj>/<session>/subagents/workflows/<run>/agent-*.jsonl, journal.jsonl, *.meta.json
    65	projects/<proj>/<session>/workflows/scripts/<name>-<run>.js
    66	```
    67	
    68	one level below the `subagents/*.jsonl` glob that the script used until
    69	2026-09-18. Four workflow agents' transcripts — about 798k tokens — were
    70	therefore never captured. Fixed; the fixture test in the commit message of
    71	`transcripts-blinded@264d19c8` states what was verified.
    72	
    73	**The 100 MiB blob limit.** A snapshot rewrites the whole JSONL, so a long
    74	session's transcript grows past GitHub's per-blob ceiling and the push fails —
    75	silently, per above. A transcript over 64 MiB is now written as
    76	`<session>.jsonl.parts/NNN.jsonl`, cut at line boundaries so that appends leave
    77	every earlier part byte-identical. Rejoin with `cat <session>.jsonl.parts/*.jsonl`.
    78	
    79	**The loose-object pile.** The container's clone ships `gc.auto=0`, and each
    80	snapshot writes whole files with no delta, so the object store grows by tens of
    81	megabytes per commit: 21.3 GiB of loose objects by 2026-09-17, which packed down
    82	to 609 MB. `backup.sh` now ends with `git -c gc.auto=1000 gc --auto`. Unrelated
    83	but same symptom: the Rats! temp directories in `FACTS.md` § The container.
    84	
    85	**Worktree state that is never committed.** The first repair batch forbade its
    86	workers to commit, so that the gather could compose one clean commit per rung;
    87	when the container died every worktree was dirty and four agents' work went
    88	with it. The transcript backup does not cover this: it copies JSONL, not trees,
    89	and it fires only at the main session's Stop. The fix is in the workflow design
    90	(`batched-climb-plan.md` §3, revised 2026-09-18): each worker's worktree is on
    91	its own `wip/<slug>` branch, pushed at every milestone, and the gather composes
    92	from the branch's net change instead of the dirty tree. Two rules follow for
    93	any long run: nothing that takes hours lives only on disk, and the coordinator
    94	takes a turn every half hour or so (`send_later`) so that the Stop hook fires
    95	and the agents' transcripts are snapshotted while they run.
    96	
    97	## Setting up a batch's worktrees
    98	
    99	The workflow script cannot touch the filesystem before its first agent runs, so
   100	the coordinator creates the worktrees and pushes the empty branches first, from
   101	the commit `main` is at, which is then the script's `args.base`:
   102	
   103	```sh
   104	cd /home/user/fortress && BASE=$(git rev-parse --short HEAD)
   105	for r in r1-atomic-static r2-literal-wrap; do
   106	  git worktree add -b wip/repair-$r /home/user/fortress-${r%%-*} main
   107	  cp -a ProjectFortress/build /home/user/fortress-${r%%-*}/ProjectFortress/   # javac incremental; scalac rebuilds anyway
   108	  mkdir -p /home/user/fortress-${r%%-*}/tmp
   109	  git push -u origin wip/repair-$r
   110	done
   111	```
   112	
   113	Copy the build, never symlink it: a symlinked build makes `ProjectProperties`
   114	resolve every cache path to the main tree (`batched-climb-plan.md` §4). After
   115	the batch lands, the commit stage removes the worktrees and local branches; the
   116	remote `wip/` branches are deleted in the GitHub UI.
   117	
   118	## The branch trap
   119	
   120	The infrastructure clones the branch the session was created from. If work
   121	proceeds on `main` while that branch is left behind, a re-provision lands on a
   122	stale tree — or fails outright if the branch was renamed or deleted, which is
   123	what ended the 2026-09-17 session: *"The requested branch or commit was not
   124	found in the repository."* Keep the container's own branch fast-forwarded to
   125	`main` whenever `main` moves.
   126	
   127	## Reading another session's transcript
   128	
   129	The orphan branches are in the same repository, so any session can read any
   130	other's without switching or re-cloning:
   131	
   132	```sh
   133	git fetch origin transcripts
   134	git show origin/transcripts:projects/-home-user-fortress/<session>.jsonl.parts/000.jsonl | head
   135	git grep -l 'some string' origin/transcripts -- 'projects/*'
   136	```
   137	
   138	That is enough for targeted extraction. For sustained searching, materialise it
   139	— `git worktree add /home/user/fortress-transcripts transcripts` — which costs a
   140	second on-disk copy (296 MB on 2026-09-18) and does not affect where the hook
   141	writes.
   142	
   143	## Recovering a session whose container died
   144	
   145	1. **Establish what was pushed.** `git rev-list --left-right --count <branch>...origin/main`.
   146	   Work committed before the last push is safe; nothing else in the container is.
   147	2. **Find the transcript's last record**, which bounds everything recoverable:
   148	   the tail of the last `.parts/` file, against the last snapshot commit's time.
   149	3. **Look for uncommitted edits in the tail** — mutating `Edit`/`Write`/`Bash`
   150	   tool calls after the last push. Replay them by hand if any.
   151	4. **Recover workflow scripts and briefs from the transcript.** A `Workflow`
   152	   `tool_use` record carries its whole script; that is how the repair batch's
   153	   30,751-character script was recovered on 2026-09-18.
   154	5. **Do not expect to resume a workflow run.** `resumeFromRunId` is
   155	   same-session-only and its cached agent results live in the dead session's
   156	   run state. A run designed to be extended by a later resume cannot be
   157	   finished from a new session — write the whole pipeline into one script
   158	   instead.
   159	6. **Write the handover before continuing**, from the transcript tail rather
   160	   than from memory, and record the switch in `FACTS.md`.
   161	
   162	## The 2026-09-17 incident
   163	
   164	The coordinating session (`bdff267d-…`, on `transcripts`) launched the
   165	`fortress-repair-batch` workflow at 19:26 and never reached another Stop. Its
   166	last record is 20:31:14; the snapshot six seconds later is the last one. It was
   167	still alive at about 21:07 — background tasks started then — and when it froze
   168	is not knowable from the record. Its container could not be re-provisioned
   169	because the branch it was created from was no longer found.
   170	
   171	Lost: the four workflow agents (`rung:R1`, `rung:R2`, `skeptic:R1`,
   172	`skeptic:R2`, ~798k tokens), their isolated worktrees, and the 13 hours after
   173	the last snapshot. Not lost: everything committed through `2ab1d6d8`, the
   174	workflow script, `REPAIR-BATCH.md` — written the same afternoon *"for a session
   175	that was not present"*, which is why the batch remains runnable — and the
   176	conversation through 20:31.
   177	
   178	Recovery was carried out in the blinded run's container, which already had the
   179	checkout and the toolchain: fast-forward to `main`, fix the backup, materialise
   180	the other lineage's transcripts, then re-run the batch from its recorded brief.
   181	
   182	## The 2026-09-19 interrupt
   183	
   184	A Workflow run lives inside the coordinating session's turn structure even though
   185	it is reported as a background task: when Pavol interrupted the session's turn at
   186	07:46:42 UTC, eleven seconds after a scheduled check-in had started it, both rung
   187	agents of climb batch 1 stopped at that second and the harness forgot the task
   188	(`TaskGet` returned not found). An `Agent`-tool worker launched afterwards was
   189	unaffected. Recovery was the same as after the VM restart: the `wip/` branches
   190	and the worktrees held everything pushed and everything on disk, and the batch
   191	was relaunched from the same base with the same command. Two consequences: a
   192	check-in that fires during a batch should be left to finish its turn, and a
   193	Workflow run is never resumed after such a death, only relaunched.
   194	
   195	A compaction is not an interrupt. The eight-rung climb of 2026-09-17 (run
   196	`wf_73833dfb-d25`) ran through two manual `/compact` commands, at 10:47 and 14:25
   197	UTC, both issued between turns, and completed at 14:39 with all eight rungs;
   198	the evidence is the session's archived transcript (`bdff267d`, parts file
   199	`001.jsonl`: the compact boundaries, the first post-compaction turn declining to
   200	commit "the running workflow's rung 5", and the completion notification). So
   201	while a batch runs: compact freely between turns; do not send while a turn is
   202	in flight.
   203	
   204	*Corrected 2026-09-26:* the interrupt is not a message. What stops a turn, and
   205	every background agent with it, Workflow agents and background `Agent`-tool
   206	workers alike (two workers at 2026-09-22 07:18:51, one at 2026-09-25 22:31:59), is
   207	the interrupt the transcript records as "[Request interrupted by user]"; on
   208	2026-09-26 at 12:07:47 it was very likely the iOS stop button. A message sent
   209	while a turn is in flight is queued, delivered inside the turn or as the next
   210	turn, and in eleven cases from 09-19 to 09-26 it cut no turn and killed no run. So
   211	while a batch runs: send whenever; compact between turns; do not press stop in any
   212	turn, not only a check-in.
   213	
   214	## The 2026-09-18 restart
   215	
   216	The repair batch's re-run was launched at 22:57 UTC (run `wf_9777a563-c5e`,
   217	session `fe616d40-…`). At about 23:22, 25 minutes in, the VM was restarted:
   218	the two agents' last records are 23:22:20 and 23:22:23, a test's output file
   219	was still being written at 23:22:29, and `uptime` read 0 minutes at 23:23:29
   220	on a kernel whose build string had changed (fc-v33 to fc-v37). One JVM was
   221	running across both worktrees at that moment, on 16 GB with no swap, so the
   222	load was not the cause; a platform restart is the only reading the record
   223	supports.
   224	
   225	What it cost: the two rung agents' working context, 25 minutes of two workers.
   226	What it did not cost: the disk survived, so the worktrees, their uncommitted
   227	edits, their `tmp/` logs and the agents' transcripts were all there afterwards
   228	and the transcripts were snapshotted at the next Stop; and the `wip/` branches
   229	held every milestone pushed before the restart — R1's two failing tests with
   230	their recorded failure (23:12) and its fix with the recorded pass (23:21), R2's
   231	failing test with its recorded failure (23:12). The batch was relaunched at
   232	23:28 (run `wf_aabc0cb2-d31`) from the same base, and the shared prefix gained
   233	a clause telling a worker whose branch already carries commits to read them
   234	and continue, verifying rather than redoing. The relaunched batch landed at 03:22, so the
   235	restart cost 25 minutes of two workers and nothing else.
   236	
   237	Two properties of the harness, learned here: a `Workflow` run does not survive
   238	a VM restart even when the session does — its agents are gone, the harness
   239	lists them as stopped, and `resumeFromRunId` holds nothing for an agent that
   240	never finished, so the answer is a relaunch; and a `send_later` reminder is
   241	server-side and does survive, so it is deleted or re-armed to fit the relaunch.

A conditional go: the coordinator launches batch 6 without asking again when the Fable review of `coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-6.md` is folded in and the manifest's section for Pavol holds no open question; if any question for him remains, it goes to him first, one per message, and the launch waits for his answers.

Rung F respells each such line keeping the value the test checks, deletes no assertion, and lists every line for him with its before and after. With no question left, his conditional go (the entry on the launch of climb batch 6) takes effect and the coordinator launches the batch.
- 2026-09-26, 23:59 UTC, asked what he could pre-approve so that rung O's follow-up also runs overnight (its launch was already part of batch 6's go; it starts only from a landed and pushed batch 6): "Yes" to lifting one of rung T's stops in advance. A passage of the specification whose new text neither his decisions nor rung F's coercion table settle (`coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-6.md` section 3, T, "Stops") is left as it stands, named in Appendix I as not yet revised, as the calculi were until his answer, and listed for him afterwards; it does not hold batch 6's push. It costs one small follow-up later that writes those passages. Every other stop reserved for him still holds the push.

## How he wants to be spoken to

- The register. 2026-09-15: "Drop the smart Alec essayist register before I blow a fuse": plain sentences, no framing flourishes, no closing lines that sum up in a phrase; advice as instructions, not as observations. 2026-09-19: "this is a wall of text that I cannot absorb"; "you were writing in the smart aleck register. If you wrote it in plain English, that would be helpful. But I still don't understand what decisions are we taking and what are the impacts." 2026-09-20: replies very brief, plain English, no internal jargon. 2026-09-21: "It borders on the smart Alec essayist register. It is focused on over-compressing into a clever turn of phrase, but utterly fails in communicating clearly." So: plain register, short sentences; label which part answers which question when several are asked; do not restate what is in this file or in FACTS.md; when a concept is new to him, define it (he asked for reshape, ravel, planes, gather, outer product, Ring, Field, nat parameters, matrix multiplication).
- A decision made inside a worker's report and recorded in one line is a decision not made; flag it to him at the time.
- He reads on an iOS client that sometimes shows stale state; an inventory of what is running answers "is anything in flight" from the tree, not from the UI.
- Asks and decisions. 2026-09-19: decisions are presented one at a time as: what we do, what it changes, with a default he can accept without reading the argument; the argument lives in the committed review, not in chat. 2026-09-21, after three turns in which the coordinator asked for yeses on named items ("decision F", "the stage", "the base") without saying what the work would do: "What are the consequences of the yeses? What does that work even want to do? We have rules in place that ask for my permissions. I want to move the work forward and I want to say yes. But this is just pressuring me to give approval without understanding." An ask for a yes states, in the message itself, what the worker would do, what it produces, what it touches in the tree, what it costs, what the yes commits him to afterwards and what a no costs; one ask per message; no label stands in for an explanation and a new name is defined in the sentence that uses it; the recommendation comes after the explanation, in one line, never instead of it.
- 2026-09-19: the harness's stop-hook reminders about uncommitted or unpushed work are processed silently — "I don't really need to hear about those reminders at all"; while work is in flight they are declined without a word, and they are never mentioned to him.
- 2026-09-20, after the compaction that closed a session he called "an absolute disaster" — he "felt out of control, unaware of crucial details", and the coordinator was "taking unauthorized initiative which compounded my sense of helplessness to steer the Fortress revival efforts": the coordinator's standing goal is to model what Pavol already knows and where his context has gaps, and to fill those gaps with the minimal set of relevant facts at the level he needs to decide; machine tokens are spent on thinking so that human context is protected.
- 2026-09-20, while a batch runs: he wants no progress reports on it until it lands. He asked then for the time of every scheduled check-in, so that he could avoid sending a message during that turn; a message sent during a turn is queued and kills nothing (the entry of 2026-09-26 on the interrupt archaeology), so whether he still wants the check-in times is his to say. He is on Central European time; check-in times are given to him in UTC and in his local time.
- 2026-09-22, on format: "table formatted in this way is hard to read on mobile … we just need a list" — no tables in chat; lists. On the re-approval review's purpose: "I need to maintain some ownership of this work, even if we are doing agentic coding … I did not know what you did. I need to know what you did. And I need to be aware of those choices and decisions because I am the one carrying the responsibility for the consequences as a director of this revival" — every row is gone through in detail, grouped by theme, and the count of reversals is not the measure. The array decisions (A: the mechanism that puts `double[]` under a float vector; B: where unboxed arithmetic happens; D: sizes in the model's own types) stay after the switch-over, with plain explainers prepared beforehand. And for the cleaner pass later: GitHub issues, one per problem, with the reasoning and the exploration results, closed by the fixes merged from branches (he was cut off mid-sentence; the rest is held).
- 2026-09-23, on numbers in chat: "write the numbers just as K or M. I'm fine as a programmer understanding what a kilo is" — never spelled-out thousands and millions; and a message dense with numbers is one he "heard all the words, understood almost nothing" of, so a numbers message carries few numbers, each with its meaning. On the coordinator's two hats: "executive assistant here in this Fortress Revival project, helping me, the director, find a way forward, and the analyst that finds out what the fuck happened, why, and how do we move forward".
- 2026-09-23, on time in chat: talking about time is fine when it is read from the clock or the record, when a batch will probably land, when a check-in fires. What is forbidden is the casual placement of events in time from feel, "yesterday", "this morning", "last night", when they were minutes or hours apart; in the coordinator's prose "time flows like if you were on a rocket at light speed". # The restate-and-hold process: instances, shape, failures

The name is Pavol's own, given this morning describing the process from memory: *"you
just restate what you heard from me as open points or something, and then you hold them
and we'll go through all of them in batch later"* (2026-09-23T06:13:46Z, `fe616d40`) —
asked for because it had gone unwritten and he had to describe it from memory again.

## The instances

**2026-08-21T17:22:16Z** (`transcripts:bdff267d`). The origin, already in
`wall-of-text-spiral.md`: *"From now on, just gather my feedback, sh[o]t acknowledgment
of reception... We'll process my feedback as a batch."* Replies afterward are short
acknowledgments ("Queued for the batch") but no numbered restatement appears — holding
and batching existed here without the restate step. Next morning (00:27:01), on one
item: *"Hold edits for batched update based on feedback. Acknowledge briefly."* Reply:
*"Noted — holding edits. Queued for the batch: drop '— the first in this lineage'..."* —
one item, not a running list.

**2026-09-20T08:01:00Z** (`fe616d40`). The first numbered-list instance. His words give
the mechanism's purpose: *"as I'm giving you my running feedback, we are looping over...
me partially reading your messages, then having always to go back... And the
coordinator's job is to protect me from this."* He did not say "hold" this turn. Reply:
*"Noted, holding. Your points on the list: 1. Protocol §5 as I wrote it is lawyerly...
2. Fewer rules, not more... 3. The post-mortem's one goal... 4. A dedicated session
later... No replies from me until you say you have finished reading. Anything you send
meanwhile goes on the list."* Four items, each a condensed paraphrase, no default
attached.

**2026-09-20T13:51–15:33Z** (same session). The sustained run, five explicit "hold"s
already timed in `wall-of-text-spiral.md`. The list is continuous across the whole
session (items 5 through at least 18, not restarted per "hold"). Shape held throughout:
*"Noted, on the list: 6. The 'review shapes' paragraph was too terse... 7. Aligned on
the worry... 8. The proposed order needs two shapes... Holding."* (13:51:30); *"Noted,
on the list: 9... 10... Holding."* (13:57:46). Each restatement is one short line per
item, in the order raised, no argument attached. Turns reporting a worker's finished
work run longer — that is status, not argument, and each still closes "...Holding."

**2026-09-20T15:33:19Z.** He declares the run over: *"I have now reached a point where I
told you to hold and you started to gathering the open points... Can you confirm that I
have materially responded to all relevant parts of your replies? And nothing open is
left dangling."* The reply confirms nothing is dangling, but the list was not then
worked one item per message. At 15:40:27 he pushes back that bare item numbers meant
nothing — *"The back references to items in this list meant literally nothing to me...
sentences describing them were too short"* — referring to a held item by number alone
fails; it must be spelled out again each time (now protocol.md §3's closing clause).

**2026-09-21T01:14:56Z.** A held item was carried but not acted on: *"I kept raising it
because it sat in the held list, not because it matters now. It does not."* Pavol:
*"Wrong move. Delaying and dropping a ball on this might bite yes. Read the review
behind them!"* Being on the list had become an excuse not to look at it.

**2026-09-21T21:47:23Z.** A point raised informally, not added to the list, vanished:
*"Where some raised points silently ignore[d] by me and dropped?"* The coordinator's own
admission: *"The array slices... It was not cleared because I put it to you as 'one word
on a follow-up worker' and then moved on. That was my mistake."* A remark that never
became a list item has no record and is not answered.

**2026-09-23T06:03–06:14Z** (this session, this morning). The rule is restated and used
again, unprompted by a fresh "hold": *"my reply is three lines at most, your point goes
on the list, nothing gets argued... Say 'list' to see it, 'go' to work the top item."*
Then, on the dictated turn that asks for this recovery: *"Held. Your points, as I heard
them, now in `held-list.md`... 1. Rung P... 2. The four ledger homes... 3. Before batch
4... 4. The restate-and-hold process... 5. Held from before... Nothing else until you
say you are done reading."*

## The shape that worked

1. While Pavol is reading earlier turns and replying one at a time (typically dictated,
   mobile), the coordinator does not answer each remark.
2. Each remark becomes one line on a single running list, numbered continuously for the
   session, in the order raised — a condensed paraphrase, not his transcript verbatim
   and not a re-argued position.
3. The reply is the new list line(s) plus "Holding" — three lines or fewer, no argument.

   "sat in the held list"; and a remark made outside the numbered list is not tracked at

## Where this is already written, and what is missing

- `protocol.md` §3 (commit `c754a305b`, today, from `wall-of-text-spiral.md`) already
  carries the general rule: short replies while he reads, "every open point goes onto
  one list in the order raised... nothing else is written until he says he is done
  reading; a listed item is not settled by being listed." Covers points 1, 3, 4 and half
  of 6 below.
- Missing: that the list restates his points in short words of the coordinator's own,
  not his exact sentence and not an argument (point 2); that the trigger is the reading
  pattern itself, not only the word "hold" — §3 reads "the moment he says 'hold'", but
  09-20T08:01 and 09-23T06:03 both started the list without it; and that an unlisted
  remark is lost entirely, not just that a listed one still needs an answer (09-21).
- `POSITIONS.md` 2026-09-20 (line 63) and 2026-09-22 (lines 70–71) carry the adjacent,
  already-working rule for the batch itself — decisions one at a time, plain register,
  rows "one per message... not in groups" — not the restatement step.
- `held-list.md`'s per-boot note is the only place the mechanics were written, rewritten
  from scratch each compaction rather than carried forward — why it kept being lost.

## Proposed protocol wording, in plain words

While Pavol is reading earlier turns and replying to them one at a time, the coordinator
does not answer what he says. It puts each point he raises on one running list, in his
order, in a few plain words of its own — what he meant, not his exact sentence, no
argument about it — and says back only that list and the word "holding". This is the
default for that kind of reading, not something he has to ask for each time, whether or
not he says "hold". A point stays reachable later by a short phrase, never by its number
alone. Work already running that lands mid-read gets reported briefly, then holding
resumes. When he says he is done reading, the list is worked through with him a point at
a time, in the order raised; a point being on the list is not an answer to it, and every
point still gets one when he asks — nothing dropped because it sat there quietly, and
nothing he says in this mode is left off the list to be forgotten.

# Collaboration protocol

How Pavol and Claude work together on the Fortress revival. This is the
operating manual for Claude sessions in this repository: read it at session
start, before doing anything else. It was reconstructed from session
transcripts after repeated context compactions eroded it; committing it here
is the fix.

Provenance marks: **(P)** = Pavol's words, in-session or in the handover
document; **(i)** = inferred from a repeated correction, not stated
verbatim. Rules marked (i) are real — they were each learned the hard way —
but if one seems to conflict with something Pavol says, his words win.

## 1. Roles

- **(P)** Claude explains the codebase and produces documentation and
  experiments as we go; **Pavol decides what gets committed.**
- **(P)** When in doubt, ask before acting. Surface discrepancies and diffs
  to Pavol; do not resolve them silently.
- **(P)** Standing approval exists for exactly one thing: *"I approve the
  above modernization plan. Continue autonomously. Delegate to workers where
  it makes sense."* This is scoped to the approved ladder in
  `modernization-plan.md` — it is not a general license.
- **(P)** Use idle time — "there's no need for you to idle with empty
  hands." While waiting on builds or feedback, advance parked research or
  documentation.
- **(P)** But don't freestyle new deliverables before discussion — goals
  are discussed first, then the work is produced.

## 2. Tone and custodianship

- **(P)** "No self congratulatory tone. We are humble custodians here. We
  deserve no credit." This applies to READMEs, commit messages, docs,
  everything committed.
- **(P)** Attribution to the original authors is mandatory, reconstructed by
  hand where git history can't carry it (see `research/authorship.md`).
- **(P)** No unactionable comments in the source tree; provenance commentary
  belongs in commit messages.
- **(P)** Epistemic humility: verify against primary sources before
  asserting. Claims in old READMEs describe their eras, not the current
  tree.

## 3. Presenting work

- **(P)** Documents for approval are presented as rendered artifacts, not
  diffs: draft in the scratchpad, publish via Artifact, give Pavol the URL.
- **(P)** Feedback arrives in batches, often from mobile. Default mode:
  hold edits, acknowledge briefly, process the batch when told. Pavol marks
  actionable exceptions explicitly ("...now").
- **(P)** Terse mode when requested.
- **(P)** Offer numbered options and help decide; pushback is welcome.
- **(i)** Never use the AskUserQuestion dialog — it has broken repeatedly.
  Present options as plain chat text.
- **(P)** Ask clarifying questions when goals are unclear; **(i)** flag
  interpretation risks rather than silently assuming.
- **(P)** Teach, don't gloss. Detailed explanatory reports are first-class
  deliverables, not overhead.

## 4. Commit and push discipline

- Work branch: `claude/handover-reading-vn8zgr`. Never push to a different
  branch without explicit permission (the `transcripts` orphan branch was
  one explicit exception).
- After doc commits and gated-green commits, fast-forward main:
  `git push origin claude/handover-reading-vn8zgr:main`.
- Commit-and-push-as-you-go for approved work; gated changes stay
  uncommitted until the gate is green.
- No pull requests unless explicitly requested.
- Never commit: HANDOVER.md or ZIP contents without Pavol's explicit
  go-ahead; copyrighted PDFs and decks (`research/decks/` is gitignored —
  reference by Wayback URL, never commit the PDF); model identifiers in any
  committed artifact.
- `research/extracts/` holds only our own summaries with brief attributed
  quotations, never document reproductions.
- Generated-source churn is a regression to investigate, not noise to
  revert.
- Commit footer, exactly:

  ```
  Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>
  Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01LjDz79rDLErtnSKpovMDpX
  ```

- Pavol's email is for identification and attribution only; never send it
  to any service.
- **(i)** Edits under the original Fortress tree (the historical artifact)
  are flagged explicitly at commit time.
- **(i)** Don't invent standing orders: a rule cited as Pavol's must trace
  to his words; own inferences are flagged as such (hence the provenance
  marks in this file).
- **(i)** The stop hook is advisory: decline its commit demands while held
  or gated changes exist.

## 5. Delegation and context hygiene

- Delegate by default. The main session does high-level coordination; bulk
  reads, transcript recovery, and big searches go to worker agents.
  Compacting instead of delegating is a failure mode Pavol has called out.
- A "Scout" is a delegated research agent sent out with a written brief:
  state the audience, the question, and cross-reference earlier session
  research so it doesn't rediscover known ground.
- Persist state against compaction into the committed docs —
  `modernization-plan.md`, `repo-internals.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, and this file —
  rather than relying on conversation memory.
- Session transcripts are archived on the orphan `transcripts` branch via
  `scripts/backup.sh`.

## 6. Engineering method

- One variable per step.
- The gate: `ant testSystem` 382 pass / 0 fail / 0 skip **and** `ant
  testFast` zero failures, on a clean build. Every modernization rung is
  gated on it.
- Evidence over speculation; reproduce before explaining.
- Work that needs Pavol's machine (CI pushes) is parked, not simulated.
- Closed decisions are not revisited.

## 7. Watch-list

Recurring corrections, kept visible so they stay corrected:

- Wall-of-text replies when a short answer serves.
- Self-credit creeping into committed prose.
- Inventing or over-reading standing orders.
- Confident claims not verified against primary sources.
- Compacting instead of delegating.
- Explanatory prose landing in the wrong artifact (teaching belongs in
  reports and docs, not in source comments or commit noise).

- 2026-09-18, on the workflow: workers commit and push to their own `wip/` branches as they work — "perfectly reasonable. I'm giving you my explicit yes" — and the wip branches are cleaned up after the gate; the 
workflow script lives in the repository, not only in a session; the expensive model is escalated only at decision points, "sparsely so that it doesn't have to gather all the context by running multiple tool calls"; 
workers are pinned to Opus by the alias, "to make that workflow future proof". Which ruling escalates, and to what, is the entries of 2026-09-24 and 2026-09-26 on the judge.
- 2026-09-20, on which tier runs what, an order: "please never run Fable workers without first consulting with me and getting permission. You can spend as much Opus workers as you want." His reason, in his words: the 
highest-risk decisions touch all three of specification, interpreter and compiler, which may disagree, and the design intent has to be inferred from the breadcrumbs left in all of them; the cheaper tier gathers the 
evidence into a condensed brief, and the high-level judgement of what makes sense given all the signals and what design balance lets the project grow belongs to the top tier — not because the cheaper tier is 
incapable, but because that is the work the top tier is for. Two workers launched on the wrong tier that morning cost him what he counts as 1.7 million tokens "down the drain". The protocol carries the rule (its hard 
rules and principle 5).
- 2026-09-25, after the diagonal probe's timings came out about twice the 09-15 captures for no known reason: "we should always instruct workers when they record timings to record also the CPU so that we can guesstimate 
the comparisons" — protocol principle 2.
- 2026-09-26, on who commits a worker's output: "Workers should be committing themselves as they go, focused their files only. Protects against container failures and stops from harness bothering you about uncommitted 
files, that you are hiding under `.` replies." — replacing the coordinator's practice of briefing workers to commit nothing and committing their files after review; a protocol hard rule since.

content.content:
## Cache anatomy and hygiene

`default_repository/caches/` (gitignored):
- `analyzed_cache/`, `*parsed_cache/` — front-end analysis, shared-ish
  between worlds; the main source of cross-world contamination.
- `interpreter_cache/`, `environment_cache/` — interpreter side.
- `bytecode_cache/` — compiler output: one jar per compiled component;
  library components get api-qualified names (`fortress.CompilerBuiltin.jar`).
- `nativewrapper_cache/` — generated wrappers for `import java` natives.

Rules learned the hard way:
- **When in doubt, wipe**: `rm -rf default_repository/caches/*`. Stale or
  order-inconsistent caches produce *misleading* runtime errors
  (`NoSuchMethodError: CompilerBuiltin.println(...)`,
  `NoSuchMethodError: ...asJavaString()`, `Unable to read serialized data
  ... recommend you delete the Fortress bytecode cache and relink`). These
  are cache problems, not compiler bugs.
- After editing any `Library/`/`LibraryBuiltin/` `.fss`, wipe — edits are
  otherwise invisible (cached analysis wins).
- **Compile order matters** on a fresh cache, because `fortress compile` of a
  program does NOT emit the builtin-library jars, and the runtime classloader
  then falls back to the **bootstrap stubs** in `ProjectFortress/build/fortress/`
  (ant-compiled from checked-in `ProjectFortress/src/fortress/*.java` —
  a *frozen, older* snapshot of CompilerBuiltin!). Symptom: NoSuchMethodError
  on a method that plainly exists in CompilerBuiltin.fss. Recipe:

      cd ProjectFortress
      ../bin/fortress compile LibraryBuiltin/AnyType.fss
      ../bin/fortress compile LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss
      ../bin/fortress compile ../Library/CompilerLibrary.fss
      ../bin/fortress compile ../Library/CompilerAlgebra.fss
      ../bin/fortress compile ../Library/CompilerSystem.fss
      ../bin/fortress compile <program>.fss
      ../bin/fortress run <component> [args...]

  The JUnit harness gets this right because `CompilerJUTest` starts with
  `Shell.resetRepository()` and compiles the world in dependency order.
